Surah 87, "al-A'la," is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Al-Dahhak said it is Medinan. It has nineteen verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (1)

It is recommended for the reciter, when he recites ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, to say after it: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." This was said by the Prophet (ﷺ), and by a group of the Companions and the Successors, as will come. Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah the Exalted has an angel called Hizqa'il, who has eighteen thousand wings, and the distance between one wing and another is a five-hundred-year journey. A thought occurred to him: "Can I see the whole Throne?" So Allah increased him by wings like them, so he had thirty-six thousand wings, and the distance between one wing and another was five hundred years. Then Allah revealed to him: "O angel, fly!" So he flew for the length of twenty thousand years, but he did not reach the top of one of the legs of the Throne. Then Allah doubled for him the wings and the strength, and commanded him to fly, so he flew for another thirty thousand years, and still did not reach it. Then Allah revealed to him: "O angel, even if you flew to the blowing of the Trumpet with your wings and your strength, you would not reach the shin of My Throne." The angel said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." So Allah the Exalted sent down: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "Place it in your prostrations." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi in his book "Kitab al-Ara'is."

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: the meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ is: magnify your Lord, the Most High. The word "ism" (name) is here extra, intended to emphasize the magnifying of the One named, as Labid said:

"Until the year is complete, then the name of peace be upon you both"

And whoever weeps for a full year has made an excuse.

The line is from an ode of his, addressed to his two daughters, whose opening is:

"My two daughters wished that their father would live, but am I anything other than of Rabi'a or Mudar?"

It was also said: declare your Lord free of imperfection, and of what the atheists say about Him. Al-Tabari mentioned that the meaning is: declare the name of your Lord free from being applied to anyone other than Him. It was also said: declare the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him free of impropriety, so that you do not mention Him except while humble and reverent, and respectful toward His remembrance. They took "ism" to mean "naming," but the stronger view is that "ism" refers to the Named itself. Nafi' related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Do not say 'in the name of Allah' (bismillah)' with 'ism' referring to the name, for the name of Allah is the Most High." Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Pray according to the command of your Lord, the Most High." He said: that means that you say "Glory be to your Lord, the Most High."

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Musa, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, that whenever they began reciting this surah, they would say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," in obedience to His command at its beginning. So it is preferred to follow them in their recitation, but "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" is not part of the Qur'an, as some people of deviation have said. It was also said that in the recitation of Ubayy it is: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." Ibn 'Umar used to recite it that way. In a hadith: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it, he would say: [Glory be to my Lord, the Most High].

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Muhammad ibn Shahriyar related to me, saying: Husayn ibn al-Aswad related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad related to us, saying: 'Isa ibn 'Umar related to us, from his father, who said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, recited in prayer ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, then said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." When the prayer ended, he was asked: "O Commander of the Faithful, do you add this to the Qur'an?" He said: "What is it?" They said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." He said: "No, we were commanded with something and I said it."

And from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: When ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Place it in your prostrations."

All of this indicates that "ism" refers to the Named, because they did not say "Glory be to the name of your Lord, the Most High."

It was also said that the first to say "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" was Mika'il, peace be upon him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "O Jibril, tell me the reward of the one who says 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High' in his prayer or outside his prayer." He said: "O Muhammad, there is no believing man or woman who says it in his prostration or outside his prostration, except that it will be heavier in his scale than the Throne, the Footstool, and the mountains of the world. Allah the Exalted says: 'My servant has spoken truly. I am above everything, and nothing is above Me. O My angels, bear witness that I have forgiven him and admitted him to Paradise. When he dies, Mika'il visits him every day. On the Day of Resurrection, he will carry him on his wing and set him before Allah the Exalted, and he will say: "O Lord, intercede for him," and Allah will say: "I have granted you intercession for him. Take him to Paradise.'"

Al-Hasan said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: pray to your Lord, the Most High. It was also said: pray with the names of Allah, not as the polytheists pray with whistling and clapping. [Al-Mukaa' means whistling, and al-Tasdiya means clapping. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Quraysh used to circumambulate the House naked, clapping and whistling, and they considered this worship."]

It was also said: raise your voice in remembrance of your Lord. Jarir said:

"May Allah disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever the pilgrims glorify Him and proclaim His greatness with a full takbir."

Qur'an 87:2–5 and the commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾. The meaning of proportioning (taswiyah) has already been discussed in (surah) al-Infitar and elsewhere [[See vol. 19, p. (224)]]. That is, He proportioned what He created, so there was no disorder (tathbij) in His creation [[Tathbij: confusion, disarray.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, He made its stature balanced. And from Ibn Abbas: He made what He created beautiful. Al-Dahhak said: He created Adam and proportioned his form. It was also said: He created (the human) in the loins of fathers and proportioned (him) in the wombs of mothers. It was also said: He created the bodies and proportioned the minds. It was also said: that is, He created the human being and prepared him for moral responsibility (taklif).

﴿Who determined and then guided﴾. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Sulami and al-Kisa'i read (qadara) with a light dal, while the rest read it with a doubled dal (qaddara). Both have one meaning: that is, He determined and matched each form with its fitting form. Then guided means He directed. Mujahid said: He determined happiness and misery, and guided to right conduct and misguidance. And from him: He guided man to happiness and misery, and guided the livestock to their pasture. It was also said: He determined their sustenance and provisions, and guided them to their livelihood if they were human, and to their pasture if they were wild beasts. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, Muqatil and al-Kalbi concerning His saying "then guided," they said: He made His creation know how the male reaches the female, as He said in (Ta-Ha): ﴿He gave everything its form, then guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], that is, the male to the female. Ata said: He placed for every creature what sustains it, and guided it to it. It was also said: He created benefits in things, and guided man to the way of extracting them from them. It was also said: "He determined, then guided": He determined for every living thing what suits it, then guided it to it, and made it know the way of benefiting from it. It is related that when a viper (afa'a) reaches a thousand years of age, it goes blind, and Allah has inspired it that rubbing the eye with fresh leaves of al-raziyanj [[Al-raziyanj: a plant which the people of Yemen call (al-simar); one of its properties is that the sap of its branches and leaves is mixed into medicines that sharpen and polish sight (see al-Mu'tamad fi al-Adwiyah al-Mufradah by the King of Yemen Yusuf ibn Rasul, published by Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi and sons, Cairo.]] returns its sight to it. So it may be in a desert, days of travel away from the cultivated land, yet it crosses that distance along its length and while blind, until it rushes into some orchard upon a raziyanj tree which it does not miss, and rubs its two eyes against it, and returns seeing, by the permission of Allah the Exalted. And the guidances of man to what is unbounded of his benefits and uncountable of his needs, in his foods and medicines, and in the affairs of his worldly life and religion, and the inspirations given to beasts, birds and creeping things of the earth, is a vast domain and a long course [[That is, far-reaching.]], which no describer's description can encompass. So glory be to my Lord, the Most High. Al-Suddi said: He determined the duration of the fetus in the womb as nine months, and less and more, then guided it to exit the womb. Al-Farra' said: that is, He determined, then guided and misguided, and he suffices with mentioning one of them, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81], (the cold being implied). It may also mean "called to faith," as in His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], that is, you call; and indeed He called all to faith. It was also said: "then guided" means He showed them through His acts to His oneness, and that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful. There is no disagreement that whoever doubles the dal in qaddara takes it from taqdir (determination), as in His saying: ﴿And He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. And whoever reads with a light dal, it may be from taqdir, and both would then have one meaning. It may also be from qadr and mulk (power), that is, He possesses things and guides whom He wills. I say: I heard some of my teachers say: "Who created and proportioned, and determined and guided" is the interpretation of the Highness that befits the majesty of Allah, glory be to Him, over all His creation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾, that is, the plants and green herbage. The poet said: [[He is Zufar ibn al-Harith. Al-damn: dung mixed with dried dung-cakes; al-thara: dust and earth.]]

"Pasture does grow upon the dung-heaps of the dust, and the grudges of souls remain as they are."

﴿Then made it dark stubble﴾. Al-ghuthaa' is what the flood casts onto the banks of the valley of grass, herbage and debris [[Al-qumash (with a dammah): what lies on the surface of the ground of crushed things; the qumash of anything is its crumbs.]]. Likewise al-ghuthththa' (with doubling). Its plural is al-aghthaa'. Qatadah said: al-ghuthaa' is a dry thing. It is said of herbs and grass when they are crushed and dried: ghuthaa' and hasheem. Likewise, what lies around water of debris is ghuthaa', as the poet said:

"As if the summit of al-Mujaymir, in the morning, of the flood and the ghuthaa' [[In the Mu'allaqah: "al-ghuthaa'". Al-Tibrizi said: al-Farra' narrated "min al-sayl wa al-aghthaa'", the plural of ghuthaa', which is rare in the mamdud form. Abu Ja'far said: whoever narrates al-aghthaa' has erred, because ghuthaa' is not pluralised as aghthaa', but as aghthiyah, since af'ilah is the plural of the mamdud and af'al the plural of the maqsur, like rahaa and arhaa'.]] is a spindle-whorl [[Tabarani: Tamiyyah is a mountain; in some copies of the Mu'allaqah of Imru' al-Qais: "as if the peaks of al-Mujaymir in the morning"; al-Tibrizi, the commentator of the Mu'allaqah, pointed to the first narration. He said: "al-Mujaymir" is land of the Banu Fazarah, and Tamiyyah a mountain in their lands. He means: al-Mujaymir has filled, so the mountain appears like a spindle-whorl in water, because the flood gathered debris around it.]]"

The lexicographers also relate: the valley ghatha and jafa'a [[In the originals: (wanjafa), which is a distortion of (jafa). Al-jufa' (like ghurab): what the valley casts out.]]. Likewise water: when there lies upon it foam and debris of no use. Al-ahwa': the black; that is, the plant verges toward dark green from the intensity of its greenness, like the black. Al-huwwah: blackness. Al-A'sha said:

"In her lips is a dark tinge, slightly black, which is pleasing; and in her gums and in her canine teeth is sweetness."

And in al-Sihah: al-huwwah is darkness of the lip. One says: a man is ahwa, a woman is hawwa', and I have become ahwa. A camel is ahwa when blackness mixes with its greenness and yellowness. The diminutive of ahwa is uhayw, in the dialect of those who say usayawid. Then it was said: ahwa may be a state (hal) of al-mar'a, and the meaning would be: as if from its greenness it verges toward blackness; the sense being: He brought forth the pasture ahwa (dark), then made it stubble. It is said: the plant has become dark (huwiya), related by al-Kisa'i, who said: "And a rain from al-Wasmi, whose hillsides are dark, I entered its depths with a tall, lusty, bold-hearted [steed]."

It may also be that ahwa is an adjective of ghuthaa'. The meaning: it became so after its greenness. Abu Ubaydah said: He made it black from its burning and age, and fresh things when they dry turn black. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: He brought forth the pasture green, then when it dried it turned black from its burning, becoming stubble which the winds and floods carry away. This is a parable Allah has struck for the disbelievers, for the passing of the world after its freshness.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾. The meaning of proportioning (taswiyah) has already been discussed in (surah) al-Infitar and elsewhere [[See vol. 19, p. (224)]]. That is, He proportioned what He created, so there was no disorder (tathbij) in His creation [[Tathbij: confusion, disarray.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, He made its stature balanced. And from Ibn Abbas: He made what He created beautiful. Al-Dahhak said: He created Adam and proportioned his form. It was also said: He created (the human) in the loins of fathers and proportioned (him) in the wombs of mothers. It was also said: He created the bodies and proportioned the minds. It was also said: that is, He created the human being and prepared him for moral responsibility (taklif).

Both have one meaning: that is, He determined and matched each form with its fitting form. Then guided means He directed. Mujahid said: He determined happiness and misery, and guided to right conduct and misguidance. And from him: He guided man to happiness and misery, and guided the livestock to their pasture. It was also said: He determined their sustenance and provisions, and guided them to their livelihood if they were human, and to their pasture if they were wild beasts. He said: "We will teach you to recite" (sanuqri'uka), meaning the Qur'an, O Muhammad, "and you will not forget" (fala tansa), meaning you will memorise it. Ibn Wahb narrated this from Malik.

This is good news from Allah the Exalted. He gave the Prophet glad tidings by granting him a clear sign: Jibril would recite to him the revelation, and he was unlettered (ummi), unable to write or read, yet he would retain it and not forget it.

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid, who said: "He used to repeat it to himself out of fear that he might forget, so it was said to him: 'We have sufficed you for it.'"

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: When Jibril brought down the revelation to the Prophet (ﷺ), Jibril would not finish the last part of the verse before he began speaking the first part to the Prophet (ﷺ), out of fear that he would forget it. So this was revealed: "We will teach you to recite, and you will not forget," meaning after that he would forget nothing, "for We have sufficed you for it."

The exception (istithna') in this reading is explained by what al-Farra' said: "Except what Allah wills," and He did not will that he forget anything. This is like His saying: ﴿They will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ (Qur'an 11:107–108), and He does not will it. It is also said in ordinary speech: "I will give you everything you ask for, except what you wish," or "except if I wish to withhold it from you," while the intention is that he will withhold nothing. On this basis, the rules of oaths are applied: an exception is made in them, and the intention of the one swearing is completeness.

In the narration of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas: "After the revelation of this verse he did not forget until he died, except what Allah willed." And from Sa'id, from Qatada, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not forget anything, except what Allah willed."

In light of these reports, it has been said: "Except what Allah wills that he forget," but he forgot none of it after the revelation of this verse. It has also been said: "Except what Allah wills that he forget, and then he remembers afterwards," so he did forget, but he would be reminded and did not forget completely.

It has been narrated that he dropped a verse in his recitation during prayer, and Ubayy thought it had been abrogated (nusikhat). He asked him, and he said: "I forgot it." It has also been said: this is from forgetting, meaning "except what Allah wills to make you forget." Then it was said: this carries the meaning of abrogation (naskh), i.e., "except what Allah wills to abrogate." The exception is a kind of abrogation.

It was also said that forgetting here means abandoning, i.e., He will protect you from abandoning acting upon it, "except what Allah wills that you abandon, because He abrogates it." This refers to the abrogation of its practice, whereas the first view refers to the abrogation of its recitation.

Al-Farghani said: The people of spiritual expansion (ahl al-bast) among the sciences used to frequent the assembly of al-Junayd, and Ibn Kaysan the grammarian used to attend it as well, and he was a man of high standing. One day he said: "What do you say, O Abu al-Qasim, concerning Allah's saying: 'We will teach you to recite, and you will not forget'?" He answered him quickly, as though the question had been put to him some time before: "You will not forget acting upon it." Ibn Kaysan said: "May Allah not open your mouth! As for His saying fala (you will not): it is a negation (li-al-nafy), not a prohibition (li-al-nahy). It has also been said that it is a prohibition. The letter ya' was retained in tansa (the alif in tansa, whose root is ya': nasiya yansa) because the verse endings (ru'us al-ay) follow that pattern.

The meaning is: Do not neglect its recitation and repetition, lest you forget it, "except what Allah wills to make you forget it" by lifting its recitation for a benefit.

The first view is the preferred one, because an exception from a prohibition is hardly ever anything but temporary and known. Also, the ya' is written in all the codices of the Qur'an (al-masahif), and the readers (al-qurra') follow it.

It has been said: the meaning is "except what Allah wills to delay sending down." It has also been said: the meaning is that He makes it "dark stubble" (ghutha' ahwa), "except what Allah wills that the children of Adam and the beasts should consume," for it will not then be as it was.

His saying: ﴿Indeed He knows what is open﴾, meaning the declared, in speech and deed, ﴿and what is hidden﴾ of the secret. From Ibn Abbas: "what is in your heart and soul." Muhammad ibn Hatim said: He knows the public and the private giving of charity. It has also been said: "what is open" is what you have memorised of the Qur'an in your breast, and "what is hidden" is what has been abrogated from your breast.

"And We will ease you" (nuyassiruka) is coordinated with "We will teach you to recite" (sanuqri'uka). The statement "Indeed He knows what is open and what is hidden" is an interjection (i'tiraD). The meaning of "to the easy" (li-al-yusra) is: to the easy path, which is doing good. Ibn Abbas said: "We will ease you so that you do good." Ibn Mas'ud said: "to the easy" means to Paradise. It has also been said: "We will guide you to the easy Shari'a, which is the upright (hanifiyya), tolerant and simple religion," as al-Dahhak stated. It has also been said: "that is, We will make the revelation easy for you, until you memorise it and act upon it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 87, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾. That is, admonish your people, O Muhammad, with the Qur'an. ﴿If the reminder benefits﴾, that is, the admonition. Yunus reported from al-Hasan that he said: "It is a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever." Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "It benefits my friends and does not benefit my enemies." Al-Jurjani said: "Reminding is obligatory even if it does not benefit." The meaning is: "Remind, whether the reminder benefits or does not benefit," so the second clause is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [[Qur'an 16:81.]] [al-Nahl: 81]. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 87, verses 14–15:

There are three issues (masa'il) here.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾. That is, he has attained to remaining in Paradise, namely the one who purifies himself from polytheism (shirk) through faith (iman). This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ata and Ikrimah. Al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: it means whoever's deed is pure and growing. Ma'mar related from Qatadah: "Tazakka" (purifies himself) means with righteous deed. And from him, and from Ata and Abu al-Aliyah: it was revealed concerning the zakat al-fitr (obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan). Ibn Sirin said: "He has succeeded who purifies himself" [means] he came out and prayed after he had paid. Ikrimah said: a man used to say, "I present my zakat before my prayer." Sufyan said: Allah the Exalted said, "He has succeeded who purifies himself, and remembers the name of his Lord and prays."

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Umar that this refers to zakat al-fitr and the Eid prayer (salat al-'id). Abu al-Aliyah likewise said this, and said: the people of Madinah do not regard any charity as more excellent than it, nor the giving of water. Kathir ibn Abd Allah related from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, "He has succeeded who purifies himself," that he said: [he pays the zakat al-fitr], and concerning "and remembers the name of his Lord and prays," he said: [the Eid prayer]. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "and remembers the name of his Lord on the way to the musalla (prayer ground) and prays" refers to the Eid prayer.

It was also said that the verse means the zakat of all wealth; this was said by Abu al-Ahwas and Ata. Ibn Juraij related: I said to Ata, "Does 'He has succeeded who purifies himself' refer to the zakat al-fitr?" He said: "It refers to all charities."

It was said further: it refers to the purification of deeds, not the zakat of wealth, meaning that he purifies his deeds from showing off (riya') and shortcoming, because the more common usage is to say of wealth "zakka" (he paid zakat), not "tazakka."

Jabir ibn Abd Allah related: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [He has succeeded who purifies himself, that is, whoever testifies that there is no god but Allah, renounces rivals, and testifies that I am the Messenger of Allah]. Ibn Abbas said concerning "tazakka": it means "There is no god but Allah." Ata related from him: it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: In Madinah there was a hypocrite who had a palm tree leaning over the house of an Ansari man. When the winds blew, they would knock down the unripe and ripe dates into the Ansari's house, and he and his family would eat them. The hypocrite disputed with him, and the Ansari complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He sent for the hypocrite, though he did not know his hypocrisy, and said: [Your Ansari brother mentions that your dates fall into his house, and he and his family eat them. Would you like me to give you a palm tree in Paradise in exchange for it?] He said: "I would sell the immediate for the deferred! I will not do it." It is related that Uthman ibn Affan gave him an orchard of palm trees in exchange for his palm tree, and concerning this it was revealed: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾. And it was revealed concerning the hypocrite: ﴿The most wretched will avoid it﴾.

Al-Dahhak mentioned that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

The second issue: we have already discussed the ruling on zakat al-fitr in full in surah al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 343 onward.] It has already been stated that this surah is Meccan according to the majority (al-jumhur), and there was in Makkah neither an Eid nor zakat al-fitr. Al-Qushayri said: It is not unlikely that He praised those who comply with His command concerning zakat al-fitr and the Eid prayer, regarding what He would command in the future.

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾, that is, he remembers his Lord. Ata related from Ibn Abbas: he means that he remembers his return (ma'ad) and his standing before Allah, the Exalted in praise, so he worships Him and prays to Him. It was also said: he remembers the name of his Lord by the takbir (saying Allahu akbar) at the beginning of the prayer, since the prayer is not valid except by mentioning Him, and this is His saying, "Allahu akbar." From this is derived the argument for the obligation of the opening takbir (takbirat al-ihram), and that it is not part of the prayer, since "prayer" is conjoined to it. There is in this an argument for those who say that the opening may be made with any of the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is a disputed issue among the jurists. The discussion of this has already passed at the beginning of surah al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 571 onward.]

It was also said: it refers to the takbirat of the Eid. Al-Dahhak said: "and remembers the name of his Lord on the way to the musalla and prays" means the Eid prayer.

It was said: it means that he remembers his Lord in his heart during his prayer, fearing His punishment and hoping for His reward, so that his completion of it and his humility in it correspond to his fear and his hope.

It was said: it means that he begins the opening of every surah with "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."

"And prays" means "and prays and remembers." There is no difference between saying, "You honored me, so you visited me," and saying, "You visited me, so you honored me."

Ibn Abbas said: this refers to the obligatory prayer, which is the five daily prayers. It was also said: it refers to supplication (du'a'), that is, calling upon Allah for the needs of this world and the Hereafter. It was also said: it refers to the Eid prayer, as said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Umar and others, and this has already passed.

It was also said: it means that he performs a voluntary prayer after paying his zakat; this was said by Abu al-Ahwas, and it is the implication of Ata's statement.

It is related from Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): Whoever establishes the prayer but does not pay the zakat, there is no prayer for him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 87, verse 16:

The common reading is "بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ" (bal tu'thirūna, "Nay, you prefer") with the letter tā' (ta). Its confirmation is the reading of Ubayy: "بَلْ أَنْتُمْ تُؤْثِرُونَ" (bal antum tu'thirūna, "Nay, you yourselves prefer").

Abu 'Amr and Nasr ibn 'Asim read "بَلْ يُؤْثِرُونَ" (bal yu'thirūna, "Nay, they prefer") with the letter yā' (ya), in the third person (al-ghaybah). Its implied subject is: "بَلْ يُؤْثِرُونَ الْأَشْقَوْنَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا" (bal yu'thirūna al-ashqawna al-ḥayāh al-dunyā, "Nay, the most wretched prefer the worldly life").

According to the first reading, its interpretation is: "Nay, you, O Muslims, prefer the accumulation of worldly things over the accumulation of reward."

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited this verse and said: "Do you know why we preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter? Because the world was present and its good things, its food and its drink, its pleasures and its splendour were hastened to us, while the Hereafter was hidden from us. So we took what was immediate and left what was deferred."

Thabit related from Anas who said: "We were with Abu Musa on a journey, and the people were talking and mentioning the world. Abu Musa said: 'O Anas, one of these people nearly tears the hide with his tongue, tearing it apart. Come, let us remember our Lord for a while.' Then he said: 'O Anas, what is it that holds back people, what keeps them from obedience?' I said: 'The world, Satan, and desires.' He said: 'No, but the world has been hastened and the Hereafter has been hidden. By Allah, if they were to witness it, they would not turn away nor waver.'"

[[Al-thabr: restraint, i.e., what prevented and kept them from obedience to Allah.]]

[[The phrase (ma 'adalu): they did not equate it with anything. And the phrase (wa la maylu): i.e., they did not doubt or hesitate (from al-Nihayah of Ibn al-Athir).]]

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 87, verse 17:**

﴿And the Hereafter is better and more enduring.﴾ (17)

That is, "and the Hereafter abode," i.e., Paradise. "Better" means more excellent. "More enduring" means more lasting than this world.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [What is this world in comparison with the Hereafter, except as when one of you dips his finger into the sea; let him look at what it returns with.] [Sahih.] This has already been mentioned [see vol. 4, p. 320].

Malik ibn Dinar said: "If this world were of gold, and it perished, and the Hereafter were of pottery, and it endured, it would still be obligatory to prefer the pottery that endures over the gold that perishes. How much more so, when the Hereafter is of gold that endures, and this world is of pottery that perishes."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: He means His saying, ﴿but the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾. And the two of them said: The Books of Allah, may His praise be exalted, have consecutively stated, as you hear, that the Hereafter is better and more enduring than this world. Al-Hasan said: As for ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾, he said: All the Books of Allah, may His praise be exalted. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ refers to His saying, ﴿He has certainly succeeded﴾ to the end of the surah, based on the hadith of Abu Dharr, as will come. Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾, he said: this surah. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an is in the former scriptures﴾, i.e., the former Books.

(The scrolls of Abraham and Moses) meaning the Books revealed to them both. It is not intended that these exact words are in those scrolls; rather it is according to the meaning, i.e., the meaning of this speech is found in those scrolls. Al-Ajurri related from the hadith of Abu Dharr, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what were the scrolls of Abraham?" He said: "They were all parables: O sovereign, domineering, afflicted, deluded one, I did not send you to amass the world, piling some of it upon others, but I sent you to turn away from Me the supplication of the oppressed, for I do not reject it even if it comes from the mouth of an unbeliever." And there were parables in them: "The intelligent person should have three periods: a period in which he communes with his Lord, a period in which he takes account of his soul, reflecting in it upon the handiwork of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, toward him, and a period in which he is alone for his needs of food and drink. The intelligent person should not travel except for three purposes: provision for the Hereafter, repair for livelihood, and pleasure that is not forbidden. The intelligent person should be aware of his time, attentive to his affairs, and guarding his tongue. Whoever counts his speech as part of his deeds will speak little, except regarding what concerns him." He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what were the scrolls of Moses?" He said: "They were all admonitions: I marvel at one who is certain of death, how he can rejoice! I marvel at one who is certain of destiny, how he can toil! I marvel at one who sees the world and its turning over its people, how he can feel at ease in it! I marvel at one who is certain of the reckoning tomorrow, yet does not act!" He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, is there anything in our hands of what was in the hands of Abraham and Moses, of what Allah has revealed to you?" He said: "Yes.
